  model pattern, optimizer, CUDA graphs, and all-rank profiler settings are unchanged. No Megatron
  implementation file changed; source commit remains `99ae923603b295c72372af85bc1bffe5c39bf8b2`.
- Submitted identical eight-node, segment-four copies as GB200-backfill job `2757394` and
  GB300-backfill job `2757395`. GB200 started first at 15:23:32 on
  `lyris[0163-0165,0171,0236,0239,0243-0244]`; GB300 started 34 seconds later and was canceled
  after 26 seconds. GB200 completed all five cases successfully in 15m19s. Every case ran eight
  finite iterations with no skipped/NaN iterations and produced all 28 requested rank traces
  (140 total). The complete printed Megatron argument blocks differ only in H, expert/dense F,
  the derived shared-expert F, and output path.
- Corrected active-GEMM results (useful routed-expert FLOPs divided by the union of concurrent
  NVJet intervals) are:

  | case | H x F | forward EP12/EP16 | backward EP12/EP16 | overall EP12/EP16 |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
  | bracketed base | 2688 x 1856 | 91.04% | 85.15% | 86.86% |
  | H-only | 5376 x 1856 | 97.33% | 85.86% | 88.99% |
  | F-only | 2688 x 3712 | 93.71% | 80.77% | 84.02% |
  | H+F | 5376 x 3712 | 106.83% | 85.05% | 90.27% |

- Forward has exactly zero NCCL overlap in every rank-step, and the two base controls agree to
  0.27 percentage points there. H is therefore the stronger forward dimension at these shapes;
  H+F selects an EP12 shape/tiling point that is modestly faster than EP16 for equal useful work.
  Backward is noisier: the identical base controls differ by 4.25 points because their expert
  GEMMs encounter different asynchronous communication schedules. In particular, all F-only EP12
  backward expert intervals overlap NCCL, so its 80.77% aggregate is not a clean isolated estimate
  of an F-axis effect and is not used as the causal conclusion.
- Splitting backward into equal-useful-FLOP classes identifies the persistent limiter. H-only gives
  97.04% dgrad but only 78.83% wgrad parity; H+F gives 97.58% dgrad but only 77.96% wgrad. The prior
  independent H+F job `2756143` gave the same result (95.54% dgrad, 78.05% wgrad), even though its
  NCCL overlap was only 6.8%/6.5% for EP16/EP12 wgrad versus 47.7%/53.9% here. Non-NCCL overlap also
  reverses between allocations while wgrad parity remains 78%. This rules out NCCL or background
  fill-kernel co-residency as the primary explanation. Wgrad accounts for about 90-94% of the H+F
  reduced-minus-full backward active-time gap.
- Exact-uniform routing gives both roles 6,048 routed assignments/GPU/MoE layer, but EP16 owns nine
  experts with 672 assignments/expert while EP12 owns twelve with 504. Forward and dgrad produce
  token-shaped outputs, so larger dimensions make each launch/tile more substantial and H brings
  dgrad close to parity. Wgrad must instead form a separate H x F gradient for both expert weights.
  EP12 therefore creates 4/3 as many gradient matrices and writes/accumulates 4/3 as much FP32
  gradient-output surface per GPU for the same useful multiply FLOPs. H/F scaling multiplies both
  that surface and FLOPs together while leaving the 504-versus-672 reduction depth unchanged; the
  wgrad efficiency ratio consequently remains near 78-81% from the 2x-product cases through H+F.
  Further H/F growth may preserve the forward/dgrad gain but is unlikely to close backward parity.
  Increasing tokens per expert (the GEMM reduction dimension) or improving grouped-wgrad handling
  is the relevant next direction.
- Artifacts are under `slurm_runs/lyris_a3b_ep16_ep12_hf_isolation/`; consolidated metrics are in
  `analysis_2757394.json`. The wrapper and analyzer are
  `scripts/nonuniform/run_lyris_a3b_ep16_ep12_hf_isolation.sh` and
  `scripts/nonuniform/analyze_ep16_ep12_hf_isolation.py`.


## 2026-08-21 - EP16/EP12 expert-GEMM dimension test

- Tested whether the routed-expert GEMM efficiency loss from reducing EP persists at EP16/EP12,
  and whether larger matrix dimensions reduce that loss. The same-allocation A-B-A uses topology
  `8 6` with TP2/CP1 (16-rank EP16 full replica and 12-rank EP12 reduced replica), 144 experts,
  exact-uniform routing, top-k 6, sequence length 2016, MBS1 and one microbatch per replica,
  true GBS14, local CUDA graphs, regular non-distributed Adam, and the four-stage `MEME` pattern
  with two MoE layers. All 28 ranks are profiled at steps 6-7.
- This setup makes useful expert work exactly equal per GPU. Every source rank sends 42 assignments
  to every expert; an EP16 expert receives 672 tokens and an EP12 expert receives 504. EP16 owns
  9 experts/GPU and executes 108 routed-expert GEMMs per step; EP12 owns 12 and executes 144.
  Both therefore process 6,048 routed token-expert assignments per GPU per MoE layer. The base case
  is H=2,688 / expert F=1,856; the high case doubles both to H=5,376 / F=3,712, increasing routed
  expert FLOPs by 4x without changing routing, token splits, kernel counts, or topology.

  all-rank trace analyzer. No Megatron implementation file changed. Jobs `2756093` and
  `2756124/2756125` stopped before training on stale harness values

  now uses the supported regular optimizer, target/scatter chunk count 1, and an all-node named
  Enroot warm. These failures produced no benchmark measurements.

  `lyris[0222-0228,0230]`, segment size four. All three cases completed eight finite iterations
  with zero skipped/NaN iterations and wrote all 84 requested traces. The analyzer hard-validates
  108/144 total routed-expert kernels and 36/48 forward plus 72/96 backward kernels in every
  EP16/EP12 rank-step.

- Useful expert FLOPs per GPU/step are 0.724153 TFLOP base and 2.896612 TFLOP high.
  The corrected metric divides useful FLOPs by the union of routed-expert kernel intervals, so
  concurrently executing kernels count once. The bracketed base result is 644.9/511.5 TFLOP/s for
  EP16/EP12, or 79.30% reduced/full efficiency. The independent base legs are 80.54% and 78.07%.
  The doubled-dimension result is 1048.9/933.1 TFLOP/s, or 88.96%, improving 9.66 percentage points
  and narrowing, but not eliminating, the reduced-EP efficiency loss.

### Why HybridEP synchronizes and available static-capacity path

- The current workload leaves `moe_expert_rank_capacity_factor=None` and does not pad expert input.
  HybridEP therefore does not know the data-dependent number of tokens each rank will receive. Its
  dynamic dispatch reads the produced count through pinned host memory so it can size the permuted
  output/handle, which inserts `cudaStreamSynchronize`. Full activation recomputation invokes this
  forward dispatch again inside `CheckpointFunctionBackward`, explaining why it appears in backward.
- Megatron already exposes a no-per-dispatch-sync path: a non-None
  `moe_expert_rank_capacity_factor` computes a static rank receive budget and makes HybridEP call
  `dispatch_with_permute(..., non_blocking=True)`. It requires the Transformer Engine op fuser.
  Over-budget traffic is detected and `PagedStashRunner` retries the iteration in dynamic dropless
  mode, preserving correctness but adding one small overflow-status all-reduce per successful step
  and an expensive rerun on overflow. The factor must be calibrated from all-rank peak receive
  counts; forced random load balancing is not exactly uniform, so a factor of exactly one is unsafe.
- Padding every expert to a fixed expert capacity also makes the count static, but changes GEMM
  shapes/work and can drop tokens, so it is a poor performance-parity experiment. The recommended
  first test is the existing rank-capacity path on matched healthy/NEP A/B runs, verify zero overflow
  and disappearance of `HybridEPDispatch` stream synchronizations, then decide whether to replace
  its per-step overflow collective with a leaner high-water-mark/static-budget mechanism.

### Backward-compute versus HybridEP synchronization clarification

- Recomputed the full backward/recompute wall span from the first to final
  `CheckpointFunctionBackward` layer scope on the existing EP16/EP12 traces. In profiler step 6,
  rank 0 spans `624.129 ms` and reduced rank 16 spans `664.320 ms`, a `40.191 ms` wall-time gap.
  This is close to the late EDP/dense-DP record arrival (`44-49 ms`), but it is not pure compute.
- Rank-16 summed expert GEMM service exceeds rank 0 by only `4.114 ms` in step 6, and grouped
  expert-backward CPU scope time by `5.400 ms`. The anomalous layer-31 scope instead grows
  `20.137 ms`, of which `19.814 ms` is one blocking `cudaStreamSynchronize` in dynamic-size
  `HybridEPDispatch`. Thus that layer's wall-time regression is almost exactly the synchronization.
- In profiler step 5, reduced rank 16's full backward span is actually `5.352 ms` shorter than rank
  0 even though its expert GEMM sum is `4.001 ms` higher, because rank 0 incurs a `42.976 ms`
  synchronization in another HybridEP dispatch and rank 16 catches up. This rules out a stable
  tens-of-milliseconds increase in reduced-rank arithmetic as the explanation.
- Correct interpretation: backward *wall time* grows because the blocking dynamic-sizing boundary
  waits for outstanding GPU/model-EP work and prevents later backward work from being submitted.
  The synchronize does not make already-enqueued kernels slower; it exposes readiness skew and
  loses host-side enqueue/overlap opportunity. The current traces show GPU work running during the
  wait, so the wait duration is not itself GPU idle and cannot be added directly to kernel time.

## 2026-08-11

### Non-divisible EP expert-placement design comparison

- The current EP32/EP28 workaround changes a true 128-expert model to 224 active experts because
  224 is the first common multiple of 32 and 28 at or above 128. This is a 75% architecture and
  expert-parameter increase, not harmless padding, and it also reduces tokens per active expert.
- **Per-replica physical padding:** keep the router and healthy replica at 128 logical experts, but
  give the EP28 replica 140 physical slots (five per rank), comprising 128 true experts and 12
  permanently unroutable dummy experts. A balanced placement has 16 ranks with five true experts
  and 12 ranks with four true plus one dummy. The logical router must remain 128-wide because its
  dense-DP parameters must have identical shapes across replicas; therefore this still requires an
  explicit logical-to-physical expert-slot map and zero padding inside token dispatch.
  - Advantage: equal physical slots per reduced rank retain most existing all-to-all reshape,
    grouped-expert, and fixed owner-layout assumptions. A padded five-slot owner layout can also
    preserve the current fixed-size Gather/EDP/Scatter scheduler.
  - Cost: 9.375% extra reduced-replica expert capacity and, on the simplest fixed-size reshard path,
    9.375% extra expert-gradient EDP/staging volume. For the six-layer `2688-1856-2688` workload,
    the 12 dummies add 718,405,632 replica-wide parameters. Each dummy-bearing GPU adds six dummy
    experts, or 59,867,136 parameters: 114.2 MiB of BF16 weights alone and roughly 1.0 GiB when
    BF16 weights plus FP32 gradients/master weights/Adam moments are resident. Dummy zero-token
    descriptors can also add grouped-GEMM launch/bookkeeping overhead. Checkpoint and optimizer
    paths must exclude or explicitly discard dummy state, and routing/loss/statistics must never
    expose the dummy IDs.
  - It does not remove active-work imbalance: the same 16 EP28 ranks still process five real
    experts while 12 process four. It only regularizes physical tensor shapes.
- **True uneven ownership:** retain exactly 128 experts. On EP28, 16 ranks hold five and 12 hold
  four; EP32 remains four per rank. This has no dummy parameter, optimizer-state, routing-metadata,
  or padded-gradient traffic and preserves a direct logical-expert checkpoint mapping.
  - Cost: replace scalar `experts_per_rank`/`experts_per_owner` arithmetic with rank counts,
    prefix offsets, owner expert-ID lists, and per-owner chunk ranges. Standard all-to-all dispatch
    must form rank splits from those offsets instead of reshaping the expert axis uniformly. The
    NEP owner scheduler and Gather/EDP/Scatter packing must support four- and five-expert owner
    payloads. DeepEP/HybridEP and inference fused paths currently assume uniform local expert
    counts and should initially be rejected unless their APIs gain ragged ownership support.
  - Active load remains imbalanced by construction: under uniform routing, five-expert ranks
    receive about 25% more expert tokens/traffic than four-expert ranks. That is equally true for
    the padding design because dummy experts receive no tokens.
- Minimum production-quality scope for either design is five core library files
  (`nonuniform_common.py`, `nonuniform_ep.py`, `moe_layer.py`, `token_dispatcher.py`, and
  `experts.py`) plus the `pretrain_hybrid.py` integration, three focused unit-test modules, and one
  small distributed correctness/performance runner. Physical padding is estimated at roughly
  300-500 core LOC because it retains fixed physical widths; true uneven ownership is roughly
  500-800 core LOC because 24 current `experts_per_owner` references and the all-to-all layout must
  become ragged. These are source-reading estimates, not committed diffs. Full Flex/DeepEP and
  inference support adds at least two more production modules and may require backend changes.
- **Recommendation:** implement true uneven ownership for the long-term path, initially scoped to
  the standard training all-to-all dispatcher and current TE grouped-MLP workload. It is more
  invasive but is semantically clean, avoids permanent memory/communication waste, and is a better
  foundation for checkpoint and distributed-optimizer support. Retain physical padding only as a
  fallback if ragged dispatcher or backend constraints prove prohibitive. Validate first on a
  small non-divisible topology such as true 16 experts with EP8/EP6 before EP32/EP28.


### Requirement update: Flex dispatcher plus distributed optimizer

- Requiring Flex dispatcher support materially changes the earlier recommendation. Current Flex
  code reshapes routing metadata as `EP * num_local_experts`, DeepEP derives destinations from one
  global expert count, and HybridEP initializes every rank with one `num_local_experts` value.
  Pure four/five-expert ragged ownership therefore cannot be passed through the current fused
  backends without changing DeepEP/HybridEP APIs and kernels to consume per-rank expert counts and
  prefix offsets.
- Requiring DistOpt does not make real trainable dummy experts attractive. DistOpt would otherwise
  allocate/shard meaningless dummy optimizer state and would need dummy checkpoint semantics. Its
  hard NEP problem is independent of divisibility: owner-layout gradients and parameters must be
  presented through native Megatron buffers, updated parameters must be scattered back to their
  physical holders, and synthetic owner slots must map to real follower parameters.
- The revised recommendation is a hybrid: retain exactly 128 logical/trainable experts with
  uneven four/five ownership, but expose 140 **virtual dispatch slots** to Flex on EP28. Pad the
  128-column router map with 12 permanently zero columns, let DeepEP/HybridEP see five slots per
  rank, remove zero dummy slots from `tokens_per_expert` before grouped expert compute, and create
  no dummy expert weights or optimizer state. The owner gradient/parameter layout can similarly
  use fixed five-slot buffers with the unused slot represented as native buffer padding if fixed
  shapes materially simplify DistOpt; this trades at most 9.375% owner-layout communication for
  compatibility without adding model parameters.
- If constrained to the two literal choices, physical padding is the practical Flex-compatible
  choice, but dummy experts should be frozen and excluded from DistOpt/checkpoints. Implementing
  pure uneven ownership end to end would require external fused-backend work. The virtual-padding
  refinement preserves Flex compatibility while retaining the main semantic and memory benefits
  of uneven ownership.
- Expected production scope rises from six files to roughly eight to ten: the existing placement,
  MoE, dispatcher, NEP, expert-checkpoint, and entrypoint files plus DistOpt/DDP buffer integration.
  The design goal is to adapt owner-layout buffers to native DistOpt and avoid modifying optimizer
  algorithms themselves. Validation must cover Flex routing/combine with zero dummy traffic,
  one real DistOpt step with matching healthy/NEP parameters on owners and followers, optimizer
  state/checkpoint reload, and performance parity on a small EP8/EP6 non-divisible case before
  EP32/EP28.

  NCCL/non-NCCL overlap, and `-2.406 ms` GPU idle. Thus `125.595 ms` (89.4% of the profiled gap)
  is additional NCCL occupancy not hidden by non-NCCL work. GPU idle does not cause the slowdown.

  spread (`29.382 ms/operation`) matches the GPU-kernel start spread (`29.390 ms`) while each
  record-to-kernel delay is only about `0.1 ms`; the delay is therefore bucket-readiness/host

  `45-49 ms` in profiler step 6. Much of this waiting dense-DP residency coexists with EDP, so
  group residencies are not additive; it represents native collective inflation caused by late

#### Reduced-replica readiness diagnosis

- A new per-layer alignment of the existing rank-0/rank-16 profiles confirms that the EDP lag is
  created before the EDP call. In profiler step 6, reduced rank 16 reaches the three EDP CPU
  records `17.371`, `44.150`, and `49.224 ms` after full-owner rank 0. The matching dense-DP
  records lag `16.934`, `45.621`, and `49.114 ms`. This is backward-progress skew, not NCCL
  launch/stream latency.
- EP12 rank 16 owns 11 experts versus eight on EP16 rank 0. Across the 23 MoE layers this produces
  878 versus 740 `AccumulateGrad` evaluations (exactly 138 additional expert-parameter readiness
  hooks), 2,121 versus 1,569 expert GEMM launches, and 506 versus 368 expert parameters across the
  three expert buckets. The reduced rank therefore has similar aggregate expert FLOPs but more,
  smaller expert operations and more host/autograd/DDP bookkeeping.
- The largest single step-6 skew increment is now identified exactly. In layer 31's checkpoint
  backward/recompute scope, rank 16 spends `19.814 ms` in `cudaStreamSynchronize` inside
  `HybridEPDispatch`; the corresponding rank-0 scope has no long synchronize and is `20.137 ms`
  shorter. This one fence moves the cumulative rank-16 lag from about `19.7` to `39.9 ms`.
- This fence is the configured HybridEP dynamic-sizing path, not NEP EDP: no static
  `num_permuted_tokens` bound is supplied, so `_HybridEPManager` leaves it as `None`, and
  `HybridEPDispatch` invokes the backend with `non_blocking=False`. The source comments explicitly
  document that this path performs a CPU synchronization to obtain the dynamic token count. The
  trace shows the synchronization draining queued GPU work, including an `ag_nvl_kernel`, before
  host backward can continue.
- The same dynamic-size fence can occasionally stall a full replica: in profiler step 5, rank 0
  spends `42.976 ms` in the same `HybridEPDispatch` synchronization and the reduced rank catches
  up. Thus the fence amplifies whichever model-EP participant/stream is late; the reduced replica's
  systematically more fragmented expert work makes it arrive late more often, but the current
  two-rank profile cannot identify the ultimate slow peer within every EP group.
- The healthy EP16/EP16 control rules out a persistent node/rank-16 confounder. Across its two
  profiled steps, rank-0/rank-16 backward-layer skew stays within roughly six milliseconds instead
  of accumulating to `44-49 ms` as it does for NEP EP16/EP12.
- Compact analysis artifacts are in the same run directory:
  `reduced_layer_skew.txt`, `healthy_layer_skew.txt`, `reduced_scope_details.txt`, and

- The changing expert-bucket count is not caused by a fixed cross-scale bucket size. Megatron
  derives the bucket-size threshold separately for each model shape from local parameter count,
  then lays out dense and expert buffers independently at whole-parameter boundaries. Full-replica
  experts per GPU change from 16 to 9 to 7 across EP8/EP16/EP32, changing both local expert-buffer

### Exact expert, attention, and gradient-bucket derivation

- The 14-layer benchmark has six routed-MoE layers. Every routed expert is a bias-free
  `2688 -> 1856 -> 2688` squared-ReLU MLP: each FC matrix has `2688 * 1856 = 4,988,928`
  parameters and each expert has `9,977,856` parameters. Routing is top-6. The EP8, EP16, and
  EP32 scale points use 128, 144, and 224 routed experts per MoE layer, respectively; this gives
  16, 9, and 7 experts per healthy/full-EP GPU. The reduced replicas hold 32, 12, and 8 per GPU.
  Each MoE layer also has one shared expert with global intermediate size 3712.
- The two attention layers are causal Transformer-Engine dot-product Flash Attention using GQA:
  32 query heads, 2 KV/query groups (16 query heads per KV head), head dimension 128, no positional
  embeddings, and zero attention dropout. The benchmark is TP2/CP1/ETP1, not CP2.
- Exact native healthy/full-rank expert bucket derivation from jobs `2649337`, `2649339`, and
  `2649340`: Megatron computes the threshold as local total parameter count divided by 16, giving
  `94,486,908`, `68,311,164`, and `60,908,412` elements. Expert parameters are individual FC
  matrices of `4,988,928` elements; the non-distributed-optimizer layout walks them in reverse
  backward order and closes a bucket only after adding a whole matrix crosses the threshold.
  Therefore full buckets contain 19, 14, and 13 matrices. The six MoE layers contain
  `6 * local_experts * 2` matrices: 192, 108, and 84. Hence EP8 is
  `192 = 10*19 + 2` -> 11 buckets; EP16 is `108 = 7*14 + 10` -> 8; EP32 is
  `84 = 6*13 + 6` -> 7. Logged bucket sizes match exactly: EP8 ten buckets of `94,789,632`
  plus `9,977,856`; EP16 seven of `69,844,992` plus `49,889,280`; EP32 six of
  `64,856,064` plus `29,933,568`. The explicit NEP expert-group settings were selected to match
  these native healthy counts within each A/B pair.

### Exact reason dense bucket count remains four

- The four native dense buckets are not forced; this is an emergent result of reverse-backward
  parameter order, whole-parameter boundaries, and two very large untied vocabulary matrices.
  Both the output and input embedding weights contain `65,536 * 2,688 = 176,160,768` local
  elements, exceeding every EP8/EP16/EP32 threshold. The output matrix appears first and closes
  bucket 1 immediately. The intervening decoder-dense region is `201,594,816`, `201,852,864`,
  and `203,143,104` elements; it closes exactly two middle buckets at each threshold. The final
  remaining decoder segment is below threshold and is combined with the input embedding because
  Megatron checks the threshold only after adding a whole parameter, producing bucket 4.
- Logged dense layouts are EP8
  `[176,160,768; 100,795,968; 100,796,064; 176,163,552]`, EP16
  `[176,160,768; 71,183,584; 71,183,680; 235,646,368]`, and EP32
  `[176,160,768; 71,613,664; 71,613,760; 236,076,448]`. Thus only the count happens to remain
  four; boundaries and payloads change. A threshold below the final roughly 59.9M-element decoder
  remainder, a different parameter order, or tied embeddings could change the count.

### Replica-local MBS interpretation for the cross-scale chart

- The current full/reduced MBS `4/1` is intentionally below proportional, not a GPU-count-proportional
  assignment. MBS is per TP/CP data lane; because a reduced replica already has fewer such lanes,
  equal per-lane MBS (`4/4`) would make aggregate replica work proportional to GPU count. Current
  NEP work decomposes as EP8 `16 + 2 = 18`, EP16 `32 + 6 = 38`, and EP32
  `64 + 14 = 78` samples, where the second term is reduced-replica work. A proportional MBS4
  assignment would instead yield NEP GBS `24`, `56`, and `120`.
- MBS1 was retained as a conservative underload after controlled EP8/EP4 sweeps showed that a
  nominally proportional reduced replica could arrive late to shared dense-DP/EDP boundaries.
  Reduced EP owns more experts per GPU and incurs finer grouped-expert launch/dependency structure;
  in the MBS2 x 7 sweep, proportional reduced work reached only `92.64%` owner parity while one
  fewer reduced round reached `99.39%`. The current chart therefore measures NEP full-owner latency
  with the reduced replica deliberately prevented from becoming the bottleneck; it is not an
  equal-GBS or proportional-load aggregate-throughput comparison.

  `3.874-4.398 ms` later, so the offset develops inside backward rather than at allocation.

  NCCL while rank 28 advances through the other owner groups.

### Final-drain GPU-idle attribution

- Reanalyzed rank 0 from EP16/EP12 all-rank profile job `2580681`. The additional backward idle is concentrated after native backward: NEP averages `16.343 ms` idle versus healthy `5.972 ms`, a `10.371 ms` delta.
- The NEP final drain itself averages about `9.97 ms` idle: descriptor materialization after the global fence contributes `3.27 ms`, serialized host submission of 72 descriptors contributes about `4.10 ms`, and retirement/native-DDP finalization before the post-train TP kernel contributes about `2.56 ms`. Pre-drain idle is close to healthy.
- The global `torch.cuda.synchronize()` lasts about `1.94 ms` but overlaps active dense-DP GPU work and directly contributes only about `0.03 ms` idle. The problem is that descriptor preparation cannot begin until after this fence; six layer batches then take about `3.56 ms` of host time while issuing only about `0.29 ms` of GPU work.
- Scatter submission is still host-serialized despite removing intermediate waits. Rank 0 traverses 72 descriptors; each participating group launch plus nonparticipant bookkeeping advances at roughly one group per `1.2 ms`, while most rank-0 Scatter kernels last only about `0.21 ms`. Rank-0 collective record-to-kernel delay is only `0.07-0.13 ms`, and paired rank 12 launches earlier and waits in NCCL, proving rank-0 host launch cadence rather than participant readiness or transfer bandwidth is the limiting factor.
- After the final Scatter, the GPU is mostly idle for `2.35-2.77 ms` while the host retires the completion event, walks six native `finish_grad_sync()` handles, completes Python bookkeeping, and reaches the next native post-backward launch.

## 2026-08-03 - Root cause of three-bucket NEP EDP overlap loss

- The corrected job `2563690` loses EDP hidden time almost entirely in bucket 2. Healthy per-bucket
  hidden time is `6.210`, `6.160`, and `4.767 ms`; parallel NEP is `5.864`, `5.859`, and
  `0.000 ms`. Bucket 2 therefore explains `4.767 ms` of the total `5.413 ms` reduction.
- Across owner ranks, healthy submits bucket-2 EDP at `233.473 ms` and its kernel starts at
  `233.556 ms` from backward start. NEP records Gather at `245.058 ms`, its kernel starts at
  `257.429 ms`, Gather ends at `258.361 ms`, and EDP is not submitted until `273.335 ms`.
- The code path explains both delays. NEP requires the `BaseMoELayer` full-backward boundary before
  `_launch_nep_dispatch_boundary_tasks`, while native DDP launches from parameter `AccumulateGrad`
  readiness. Its Gather stream then waits on the full-boundary `compute_ready_event`, placing the
  final Gather after the final model-EP work instead of at native bucket readiness.
- Split host phases do not submit EDP when Gather completes. They are progressed only when
  `_wait_for_nep_dispatch_launch` runs at a later MoE pre-hook or final drain. For bucket 2 this
  leaves `14.974 ms` on average between Gather completion and EDP host submission; the subsequent
  record-to-kernel gap is only `0.093 ms`, proving that this part is host scheduling, not NCCL skew.
- Replaying the same NEP EDP durations at healthy launch offsets increases modeled hidden time from
  `11.724` to `15.696 ms`, recovering `3.972 ms` (`73.4%`) of the hidden-time deficit. The primary
  cause is therefore late NEP readiness/submission, not lack of useful backward work.
- A complete fix must launch Gather from bucket parameter readiness and progress EDP as soon as its
  Gather dependency is satisfied. Progressing EDP earlier without moving Gather earlier can recover
  little because the final Gather itself is already behind the useful overlap window.

## 2026-08-03 - Bounded parallel owner-Gather submission

- Added an opt-in `MEGATRON_NONUNIFORM_EP_PARALLEL_GATHER_WINDOW`; its default value of `1`
  preserves the existing single ordered dispatch stream. A value of `2` starts at most two
  independent owner waves on separate CUDA streams and joins their completion events before the
  direct-Scatter completion boundary. Focused container validation passed Black, isort, Python
  compilation, and `30` tests (`88` deselected).
- EP8/EP4 job `2562618` passed exact gradient checksums, but its Gather process groups are disjoint
  pairs and form only one owner wave, so it could not test this change. Its serial/parallel timing
  difference was treated as allocation drift rather than evidence.
- EP16/EP12 GB200 job `2562746` completed `0:0` on contiguous nodes `lyris[0217-0224]`. This is the
  smallest tested topology with three overlapping owner waves (`[0,12]`, `[4,12]`, `[8,12]`). The
  exact two-iteration gradient checksum gate matched all fields with zero relative delta.
- Same-allocation timing, iterations 4-10: serial `580.500 +/- 2.839 ms`, parallel-two
  `579.043 +/- 2.399 ms`, and serial repeat `578.914 +/- 3.887 ms`. Parallel-two is `0.664 ms`
  (`0.115%`) faster than the midpoint of the two serial legs, which is below run variance and is
  not a measurable iteration-time improvement.
- All-rank profiles show that the bound works as designed. On shared follower rank 12, the second
  wave is submitted about `0.9 ms` after the first instead of about `99 ms`; participant kernel
  start spread for `[4,12]` falls from `6.392` to `1.338 ms`. The third wave remains around `98 ms`
  behind the first because window two intentionally admits only the first two waves; its start
  spread falls from `13.940` to `7.113 ms` through earlier downstream progress.
- Parallel submission introduces real collective contention: average rank-12 summed Gather kernel
  residency rises from `7.428` to `10.136 ms` (`+36.5%`) while `3.202 ms` runs concurrently. The
  union still decreases from `7.428` to `6.934 ms` (`-0.494 ms`). Gather overlap with native
  model-EP changes only from `2.466` to `2.548 ms`, and full-replica model-EP matched service is
  unchanged (`47.480` versus `47.397 ms`), so there is no evidence that this window penalizes
  Megatron model-EP A2As. The bounded experiment fixes launch skew, but bandwidth sharing and the
  still-serialized third wave leave too little critical-path gain to improve iteration time.

## 2026-07-30 - Backward-complete Scatter drain

- Confirmed that owner Gather already uses `dist.all_to_all_single(..., async_op=True)` in the
  overlap path. The long owner-side Gather kernels observed in traces are device-side NCCL
  participant waits when follower ranks arrive later; only EDP for the same owner chunk depends
  on the Gather output. Independent backward compute has no data dependency on its completion.
- Confirmed that `MEGATRON_NONUNIFORM_EP_NCCL_SCATTER_CHUNKS` partitions Scatter descriptors
  after the corresponding whole owner EDP operation. It does not partition Gather or EDP into a
  per-chunk `Gather -> EDP -> Scatter` pipeline. During backward, those Scatter descriptors are
  submitted through model-EP A2A windows; the old final drain incorrectly synchronized each
  remaining descriptor before submitting the next one.
- Added an explicit backward-complete scheduler state. Final drain now consumes any outstanding
  ordered-window ticket once, queues every remaining Scatter descriptor behind the preceding
  Scatter stream dependency, and performs one final completion wait. The next backward clears
  the completed state before its first model-EP A2A burst.
- GB300 job `2538157` failed in container preflight because four unit-test doubles constructed via
  `__new__` lacked the new state attribute. State reads now default to backward-active for such

  isort, compile, and focused unit preflight passed. The two-iteration EP8/EP4 checksum comparison

In the 16 setting, healthy and NEP source buffers build four non-expert buckets and seven native expert buckets; at the 4 setting they build two and two. NEP then removes the native expert params from their source groups and replaces them with the fixed three Approach-A expert groups, so its Gather/owner-EDP/Scatter readiness granularity remains three while healthy loses five native expert readiness points. This predicts that the 16 setting can help healthy more than NEP, reducing owner-parity at the 4 setting. The recorded `1.685`-point difference is not causal proof because jobs `2489678` and `2506439` used different 16-node allocations and only the 16 setting has an all-rank trace. A four-leg same-allocation bracket is required to quantify the effect and its exposed-communication attribution.

They submit exactly one Scatter descriptor only when all participants report the same ready ticket; a mismatched ticket raises a deterministic error instead of entering NCCL with divergent ordering. ### Bucket-group Scatter-window scheduler

- The EP32/EP28 profile `2487165` showed that the one-descriptor ticket pipeline was not progressing with scale: only `2/84` N=1 Scatter descriptors submitted during backward and `82` entered the final drain. The drain averaged `27.732 ms`, including `21.288 ms` GPU idle, and accounted for `96.6%` of the enlarged post-model-EP tail.
- Root cause: each model-EP boundary admitted at most one descriptor and immediately launched its next agreement. That agreement usually captured the prior descriptor as locally busy, so the following boundary consumed stale busy state even when the Scatter had already completed. More owners therefore increased the number of boundaries required rather than the amount of work admitted per boundary.
- Replaced one-descriptor tickets with deterministic bucket-group windows in `megatron/core/distributed/nonuniform_ep.py`. One asynchronous Gloo agreement now validates the descriptor count plus first/last ticket for one `(layer, expert bucket group)` window. On unanimous agreement, every owner/chunk descriptor in that window is queued in fixed order on the existing Scatter stream; queueing can cross owner-batch boundaries without bypassing stream dependencies. An explicit layer ordinal prevents one-bucket models from merging adjacent layers.
- The deterministic non-MoE CUDA-graph post-hook now finishes any ready split host phases and refreshes the aligned window pipeline after useful compute is enqueued. Model-EP burst hooks retain the one-boundary asynchronous pipeline. No rank-local elapsed-time decision controls collective count or order, and a queue/window mismatch raises before NCCL submission.

Final GB200 preflight `2488233` passed Black, isort, Python compilation, and `29` selected scheduler tests (`86` deselected), including cross-owner windowing, group/layer boundaries, cross-batch stream queueing, mismatch rejection, and compute-hook progression. Earlier preflight `2488170` stopped at formatting, and `2488221` passed the prior `28`-test selection before the window test was renamed into the standard filter.

## 2026-07-22 - Deferred-Scatter joint gap capacity

- Added `scripts/nonuniform/analyze_nep_scatter_gap_capacity.py` and analyzed the all-rank 14-stage deferred-fence trace from job `2443206`: `slurm_runs/lyris_a3b_ep8_ep4_reshard_cause_ab/deferred_no_check/a3b_repeat14_ep8_ep4_mbs1_mb1_1_proportional/2443206/torch_profile`. The reproducible result is `slurm_runs/lyris_a3b_ep8_ep4_reshard_cause_ab/scatter_gap_capacity_2443206.json`.
- The analysis uses the first two Scatter phases, where later model-EP work exists. For each `[owner, follower]` transfer pair it intersects both ranks' clocks from the later Scatter-kernel start to the earlier next-Gather start. Across eight pair/phase windows, both participants have no native model-EP NCCL kernel resident for `40.73%` on average (range `24.63-57.12%`) and neither participant has any NCCL kernel resident for `31.74%` on average (range `21.95-51.43%`).
- Strict jointly no-NCCL capacity is `4.329-13.933 ms` per window, versus `1.978-2.064 ms` owner-side Scatter residency, or `2.19-6.94x` the current transfer time. Every window has three to five strict gaps at least `0.5 ms`; every window has one to three gaps at least `1.0 ms`. The largest strict gap is `1.008-5.659 ms`. Thus enough aggregate capacity exists, but the smallest windows cannot reliably accommodate one monolithic approximately `2 ms` Scatter without colliding with EP.
- This run already used `HIGH_PRIORITY_STREAM_GROUPS=ep` and `CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=32`; native EP and owner-transfer execute on distinct streams (rank 0 streams 7 and 52), while `nep_owner_transfer` remains default priority. Priority alone did not protect EP because each Scatter kernel was already resident when the next owner-rank EP A2A arrived, by only `0.0019-0.0045 ms`.
- The transfer pairs also expose a scheduling caveat. Followers launch Scatter `4.268-8.305 ms` before owners and remain resident for `6.306-10.380 ms`, while owner kernels are approximately `2.0 ms`; paired kernels finish together. This residency includes participant waiting, not continuous link transfer. Scatter uses a 32-block, 640-thread NCCL SendRecv kernel, so the first low-priority chunk remains non-preemptible and can occupy SMs while waiting even if later chunks yield at finer boundaries.
- Conclusion: the trace supports a Scatter-only chunking experiment at `N=2` and `N=4`, preserving the existing Gather and native EDP paths and identical collective order on both participants. This is distinct from the earlier whole-reshard chunking attempt. The A/B must verify gradient correctness, unchanged native model-EP matched service, reduced Scatter/model-EP overlap, and unchanged total Scatter service. PyTorch traces contain no NVLink throughput counters, so these are NCCL-residency bounds rather than a claim of measured physical-link utilization.

- Added the memory-bounded all-rank analyzer `scripts/nonuniform/analyze_exact_uniform_nep_slowdown.py` and analyzed all 16 profiled steps on all 16 healthy and 12 NEP ranks from job `2463417`. The profiler changes absolute timing, so these traces are used for causal attribution rather than the production effect size.

Healthy native expert EDP already has `7.163 ms` exposure, so the incremental exposed reshard versus healthy is `18.480 ms` (`10.600 ms` extra EDP exposure plus `7.880 ms` new Gather/Scatter exposure).

NEP owner EDP carries exactly twice the healthy owner payload (`1,915,748,352` versus `957,874,176` elements) and matched service rises `7.736 -> 15.295 ms`. The six owner-transfer all-to-alls add `11.601 ms` matched service with only `0.206 ms` accumulated owner participant wait. Native model-EP matched service improves slightly (`5.709 -> 5.453 ms`) and TP is unchanged/slightly faster (`0.922 -> 0.846 ms`), excluding those transports as the regression source.
- The owner-layout staging path adds `801` dispatch-stream GPU operations and `9.680 ms` residency per backward: `576` DtoD copies (`4.741 ms`), `192` accumulation adds (`2.428 ms`), six fills (`0.998 ms`), six gradient norms (`1.448 ms`), and small residual work. Their overlap with existing kernels limits the exact non-NCCL union increase to `8.341 ms`, but this is still deterministic NEP-only work on the critical path.
- The implementation explains why the reshard remains exposed. This run enables split host phases but disables post-graph progression and model-EP fence deferral. Gather is launched from the MoE backward boundary on the dispatch stream, then owner EDP and Scatter are queued behind it. At the next MoE backward pre-hook, `_wait_for_nep_dispatch_launch()` orders the compute stream behind the whole completion event. Gather therefore overlaps only `3.722 ms` of remaining work; owner EDP and Scatter cannot extend into subsequent MoE backward compute. Participant-aligned model-EP milestones acquire their lag exactly at the first two reshard boundaries (`-2.919 -> +18.477 ms` and `+12.706 -> +28.890 ms`), followed by another approximately `15.9 ms` final reshard tail after the last model-EP operation.

Its payload and operation count are unchanged, but owner participant wait rises `1.929 -> 16.733 ms` and matched service rises `6.547 -> 8.580 ms`; the latter coincides with `3.353 ms` of NEP owner-EDP/dense-DP overlap and SM contention. Reduced ranks 8 or 10 are latest for `70/96` dense operations. Exact-uniform EP4 still launches `1,152` expert GEMMs per step versus `576` on EP8; reduced grouped-backward host scopes take `22.301` versus `12.790 ms`, while summed GEMM residency changes only `14.667` versus `12.268 ms`. This deterministic launch/dependency overhead creates cross-rank phase skew and moves dense-DP waiting earlier, but the reduced ranks finish backward before full owner rank 0 and do not replace the exposed owner reshard as the main bottleneck.
- Conclusion: exact routing, same-allocation ABBA timing, disabled energy/diagnostic logging, and all-rank participant alignment exclude routing imbalance, iteration variance, native model-EP transport, and TP transport as primary explanations. The dominant correct optimization target is the implementation-imposed reshard completion fence, followed by owner-layout staging overhead; any follow-up must preserve collective ordering, gradient correctness, and native Megatron NCCL service.

Because the healthy controls themselves shifted by `6.3 ms` between launches, the same-allocation ABBA comparison is the primary result and no cross-allocation variance improvement is claimed.
- All-rank traces verify that routing remained exactly controlled. Healthy EP8 has `18,432/18,432` split vectors equal to `[3072] * 8`. Profile rank-0 step means are `129.385 ms` healthy and `165.974 ms` NEP, consistent in direction with the unprofiled slowdown, but profiler-step variance is not used for the primary variance claim.

Critical-rank model-EP residency supplies the largest NCCL increase (`22.566 -> 26.997 ms`). This is waiting residency, not slower transport or extra GEMM work.

Expert-DP matched service is `0.682/0.680 ms` per operation balanced/natural and dense-DP service is `1.584/1.545 ms`; max-group service per step is likewise stable. Raw DDP residency varies with which early rank becomes critical, but service after all participants arrive does not increase. ## 2026-07-21 - Final owner-EDP rank-8 delay attribution

- Verified the exact topology from job `2443953`: ranks `0-7` are full replica 0 and ranks `8-11` are reduced replica 1. Rank 8 is therefore a reduced-replica owner; its TP group is `[8, 9]` and its owner-EDP group is `[0, 8]`.
- Rank 8 is not late at the host EDP-launch rendezvous. It enters `nep_split_wait_edp_launch` `1.923 ms` before rank 0 and waits `2.001 ms`; rank 0 reaches the pair barrier last. Native DDP then records the final EDP collective at rank-0-relative `+0.455 ms`, but rank 8's NCCL kernel does not begin until `+3.345 ms`, leaving a `2.890 ms` enqueue-to-device delay. Rank 0's corresponding delay is only `0.087 ms`.
- The device timeline identifies the dependency. Rank 8's TP peer rank 9 launches the two preceding CUDA graphs `7.599/7.628 ms` after rank 8. Rank 8 consequently enters the first TP all-gather at `-1.255 ms`, while rank 9 enters at `+1.014 ms`; both finish at approximately `+1.076 ms`, so `2.269 ms` of rank-8 residency is participant wait. A later TP all-gather similarly starts at `+2.721/+3.124 ms` on ranks 8/9 and completes at `+3.193 ms`. The final EDP kernels on ranks 8 and 9 then both start at `+3.345 ms`. This is the direct reason rank 8 reaches owner EDP after rank 0: its already-enqueued TP graph cannot advance until rank 9 catches up.
- Rank 9's immediate source of skew is one expert `_GroupedLinearBackward` operation, sequence `2725`: its host scope is `8.145 ms` versus `2.029 ms` on rank 8, accounting for `6.116 ms` of the final graph-launch gap. Every reduced rank launches 64 kernels for this operation; rank 9 has less summed kernel residency than rank 8 (`0.790` versus `1.292 ms`), excluding extra expert math as the explanation. The same rank-9 outlier exists in both controls (`10.028/9.110 ms` versus rank-8 `2.167/2.103 ms`) with `6.260/8.104 ms` final graph-launch skew, so host-progress scheduling did not create it.
- The candidate differs by enqueueing EDP while this pre-existing TP skew is unresolved. In both controls, rank 8's final EDP is enqueued only after the TP graph drains and starts within `0.084-0.085 ms`; in the host-progress candidate it is enqueued earlier and waits `2.890 ms`. The remaining internal cause of rank 9's long grouped-linear host scope is not represented by GPU work or CUDA-runtime time in the trace: CUDA runtime calls total only `0.164 ms`, with event-query clusters inside an otherwise opaque Transformer Engine scope. Distinguishing TE host scheduling from OS thread descheduling requires TE-side markers or CPU scheduler/stack profiling; neither is present in the saved trace.

- Audited printed arguments exhaustively. Apart from the intended world/DP/GBS, nonuniform topology/mode, profile-rank list, and output paths, every printed model, graph, DDP, routing, and runtime argument matches. Both cases use the same allocation and map full-replica ranks 0-7 to the same first two nodes at four GPUs per node. Parameter-norm and zero-count logging are disabled, manual GC is outside the measured range, stderr is empty, all traces are complete, and all iterations are finite with zero skips/NaNs.
- Routing is not the cause. Mean per-dispatch rank CV is `0.663%` in healthy full EP8, `0.720%` in NEP full EP8, and `0.542%` in reduced EP4; aggregate rank CV is `0.369/0.382/0.344%`. Mean routed assignments are exactly `24,576` per rank/dispatch in every group, and healthy/NEP full-replica model-EP payload differs by only about `0.07%` from random routing realization.
- The clean unprofiled gap and the profiled iteration are separated deliberately. `ProfilerStep#3` is `214.237/232.444 ms`, only an `18.207 ms` gap, and includes a different post-training logging tail. The owner backward path from its first model-EP kernel to the first dependent post-training TP kernel is `89.595/109.775 ms`, a `20.180 ms` NEP gap that closely matches the unprofiled `21.955 ms` regression.
- The backward gap has an exact interval decomposition on full owner rank 0: NEP adds `6.686 ms` of non-NCCL union and `13.945 ms` of NCCL union, loses `2.383 ms` of NCCL/non-NCCL overlap, and has `2.835 ms` less GPU-idle spacing. `6.686 + 13.945 + 2.383 - 2.835 = 20.179 ms`, matching the measured `20.180 ms` trace gap to rounding.
- NEP Gather + owner EDP + Scatter occupies `25.503 ms` on rank 0. Only `3.321 ms` (`13.0%`) overlaps useful non-NCCL kernels, so `22.182 ms` is exposed on that rank. The six matched owner-transfer all-to-alls require `10.951 ms` of true service. The three owner EDP all-reduces require `13.967 ms`, versus `7.645 ms` for healthy native expert EDP; owner EDP carries exactly twice the healthy per-owner payload (`1,915,748,352` versus `957,874,176` float elements) because gradients for 32 experts are concentrated on each surviving owner instead of 16.
- Global model-EP completion milestones show where this time enters the critical path. Before the first reshard, after backward model-EP operation 23, NEP is `5.259 ms` ahead of healthy when both are normalized to backward entry. At the next model-EP dispatch it is `4.482 ms` behind, a `9.741 ms` swing across the first reshard boundary. The second boundary raises the lag to `12.464 ms`; later model compute recovers part of it, leaving `6.167 ms` at the final model-EP completion, and the final reshard/native drains raise the backward gap to `20.180 ms`.
- Native model-EP transport itself is not slower. Across all 36 matched full-replica collectives, service after the last participant arrives is `5.808 ms` healthy versus `5.879 ms` NEP. Rank-0 model-EP residency grows `28.057 -> 50.351 ms` only because rank 0 arrives earlier than another participant and spins; comparing rank-0 NCCL residency without all-rank alignment double-counts propagated skew and is not a causal transport measurement.
- The NEP dispatch stream adds `9.959 ms` of non-NCCL work: `4.760 ms` across 576 device copies, `2.644 ms` across 192 accumulation adds, `0.998 ms` of buffer fills, `1.466 ms` of gradient-norm kernels, and small checks. Relative to healthy, the owner has `+3.790 ms` DtoD copies, `+2.647 ms` adds, and `+1.014 ms` fills before the post-training boundary; expert GEMM deltas on the full owner are negligible by comparison.
- Native DDP's finite-gradient check is an implementation-level overlap blocker in the synthetic owner EDP group. The first `nep_native_ddp_start_grad_sync` scope lasts `8.590 ms`; `7.783 ms` is `aten::item()` -> `cudaStreamSynchronize` while model-EP and Gather are queued on the NEP path. The autograd thread cannot submit later backward compute during this synchronization. This follows directly from `_ParamAndGradBucketGroup.start_grad_sync()` calling `check_grads()` and `check_grads()` reducing each bucket norm before the asynchronous all-reduce.
- NEP also interferes with existing native dense-DP communication. The final 176,163,552-element dense-DP collective has `4.060 ms` matched service in NEP versus `1.717 ms` healthy. It overlaps the final owner EDP kernel for about `2.31 ms`, almost exactly its `2.343 ms` service inflation; the other three large dense-DP collectives add only about `0.40 ms` combined. The differing six-rank/eight-rank dense-DP topology remains a small unavoidable comparison difference, but it does not explain the final inflation.
- Proportional EP4 fragmentation is real but secondary in this clean pair. Reduced EP4 executes 1,152 expert GEMMs averaging `16.151 ms` total versus 576 and `11.409 ms` on NEP full EP8. However, reduced owners reach the first two owner-EDP rendezvous `2.1-10.8 ms` before full owners. They are only `2.8-4.4 ms` late at the final rendezvous; rank 0's `4.425 ms` host wait is covered by already-running dense-DP NCCL, and the actual final EDP kernel launch spread is `0.632 ms`. Fragmentation therefore is not the primary source of the `21.955 ms` owner regression.
- Superseding conclusion for this clean default-top-k case: the proportional slowdown is primarily exposed Gather/owner-EDP/Scatter work plus NEP packing/check kernels, with loss of useful overlap and about `2.34 ms` of native dense-DP contention. It is not caused by raw model-EP bandwidth, routing imbalance, power/placement drift, or owner expert-GEMM efficiency. The current pre-hook fence orders each completed reshard before the next model-EP boundary, and the synchronous finite check delays host submission, so the available intervening compute hides only about 13% of reshard residency.
- Added `scripts/nonuniform/analyze_topk6_proportional_slowdown.py` to reproduce the timing, backward union accounting, all-rank collective service, model-EP milestones, owner-transfer/EDP payloads, dispatch-stream cost, and useful-overlap measurements. `python3 -m py_compile` and the analyzer run pass. The required `uv run isort` command could not run because `uv` is not installed on this login environment; imports are already in standard-library order.

Prior balanced job `2438661` on `nvlblk13` measured `952.23/1018.83 ms` healthy/NEP, while job `2439279` on `nvlblk06` measured `953.17/962.70 ms`: healthy differs by only `0.10%`, but NEP improves by `5.51%`. Driver topology, batch, graph, NCCL, routing, image, loss values, and the mounted NEP implementation are identical; routing CV and expert-kernel counts also match exactly.

Prior/current reduced target arrival is `1017.724/899.718 ms`; reduced model-EP residency is `143.498/95.167 ms`; and no-GPU-event spacing is `225.956/148.841 ms`. Across all reduced ranks, the same model-EP `ncclDevKernel_SendRecv` kernels average `569.4 us` on block 13 versus `377.6 us` on block 6. Full-EP8 model-EP residency remains essentially unchanged (`123.664/122.350 ms`).

SLURM history shows both 18-node NVL72 blocks were shared with other jobs, so allocation count alone does not explain it. PyTorch traces cannot distinguish persistent block health/routing from workload-specific fabric contention. Performance comparisons must keep healthy and NEP cases in one allocation, record `nvlblk`, and use exact-node/block repeats for cross-allocation claims. Job `2439279` satisfies the same-allocation requirement, so the top-k 6 versus 8 comparison is protected from this confound.

- Deeper cross-rank trace alignment shows the native inflation is primarily displaced synchronization wait, not direct SM contention. Rank-0 model-EP has `0.0 ms` direct overlap with NEP Gather/EDP, yet rank-0/rank-4 launch skew within the identical EP group `[0..7]` grows from `0.661 ms` healthy to `1.364 ms` NEP on average and from `7.696` to `14.633 ms` maximum; collective completion differs by only about `6 us`. In the clearest event, rank 4 launches `14.633 ms` before rank 0 and its NCCL kernel remains resident `14.850 ms` versus rank 0s `0.204 ms`, ending together. Dense-DP sampled-rank start spread similarly grows `1.947 -> 3.637 ms` average and `4.358 -> 9.888 ms` maximum while completion remains aligned within `29 us`.
- Mechanism: owners execute Gather plus EDP while followers execute only Gather. The normal Scatter barrier/all-to-all is also the post-EDP rendezvous that realigns them. Skip-Scatter removes that rendezvous, and the per-layer completion fence lets each local compute stream continue as soon as its role-specific completion event fires. The next model-EP or dense-DP collective becomes the first common rendezvous, so early ranks spin inside native NCCL until slower owners/replicas arrive. Only `3.077 ms` of dense NCCL overlaps NEP traffic over two rank-0 profiled steps, making direct EDP resource contention secondary to this arrival-skew transfer.
- Owner-only accounting corrects the aggregate interpretation. Full-replica owner rank 0 averages `177.734 ms` healthy versus `219.470 ms` skip-Scatter across the two profiled steps: `+41.736 ms` or `23.48%` slower. Reduced-replica owner rank 8 averages `177.690 -> 219.456 ms` (`+41.766 ms`, `23.51%`), with both owner traces ending together. The clean rank-0 acceptance steps show `135.45 -> 171.00 ms` (`+35.55 ms`, `26.25%`); profiler perturbation accounts for the different absolute gap.
- Rank-0 direct owner work is material: Gather is `6.924 ms/step`, owner-side DtoD copies add about `3.193 ms/step`, and the extra accumulation/scaling/fill kernels add about `4.62 ms/step`; owner EDP itself rises only `0.396 ms/step` relative to healthy expert-DP. Native model-EP residency rises `18.108 ms/step` and dense-DP residency `19.365 ms/step`, but these are not simply additive with direct work. Cross-rank alignment gives owner-wait lower bounds: rank 0 waits for profiled follower rank 4 inside model-EP for `22.163 ms/step` versus `10.640 ms` healthy (`+11.523 ms`), and waits for later sampled dense-DP participants for `11.086` versus `2.671 ms/step` (`+8.415 ms`). Thus at least about `19.94 ms/step` of the full owners regression is actual rank-0 waiting, not residency charged only to an early follower. Unprofiled ranks 1-3/5-7 may account for additional wait.
- Reduced owner rank 8 is not the throughput limiter: its model-EP residency falls `17.714 -> 10.168 ms/step` and EDP falls `20.418 -> 16.857 ms/step`; it has no Gather. Its equal step wall time comes from dense/global synchronization with the slower full replica. The critical optimization target remains full owner rank 0 and its peer owners in ranks 1-3.
- Exact sampled causal chain: for dense-DP bucket 4, ranks 0/4 launch at `+0.000/+1.238 ms` but reduced owner rank 8 launches at `+9.888 ms`; durations are `11.977/10.677/2.066 ms` and completion aligns. Before joining, rank 8 spends `7.513 ms` in ordinary reduced-replica GPU compute plus `0.478 ms` in TP communication. Rank 4 is consequently still resident in that dense all-reduce when full owner rank 0 launches the following model-EP collective; rank 4 joins `8.018 ms` later, so rank 0s model-EP kernel lasts `8.026 ms` versus rank 4s `0.010 ms` and they finish together. The wait therefore propagates reduced-owner compute -> mixed dense-DP group `[0,2,4,6,8,10]` -> full-replica follower rank 4 -> model-EP group `[0..7]` -> full owner rank 0.
- Other sampled rank-0 model-EP waits have the same structural cause but a different immediate late peer state: rank 4 is still executing prior MoE expert GEMMs and token sorting for gaps of `6.791`, `5.794`, `4.502`, `4.142`, and `3.103 ms`. Rank 4s total local compute changes little (`69.577 -> 70.204 ms/step`), so those are primarily phase shifts propagated from earlier synchronization, not substantial extra follower work. Reduced owner rank 8 does have materially more local residency (`70.230 -> 79.457 ms/step` non-collective kernels and `0.929 -> 7.199 ms/step` DtoD copies): EP4 places 32 experts/GPU instead of 16 and uses half the replica batch, preserving nominal tokens/GPU but fragmenting them across twice as many smaller expert operations and adding owner-buffer work.
- A deeper operator-level check corrects the phrase "ordinary reduced-replica GPU compute" in the sampled dense-bucket chain. The `7.513 ms` immediate window on rank 8 is primarily vocabulary-parallel cross-entropy forward/backward plus output-projection backward and its TP all-gather/reduce-scatter; dense bucket 1 contains `module.output_layer.weight`. Those kernels are not materially slower on rank 8: cross-entropy forward spans `5.649 ms` on rank 8 versus `5.650/5.690 ms` on ranks 0/4, and cross-entropy backward sums `1.412 ms` versus `1.414/1.425 ms`. Rank 8 instead starts the loss GPU work at `59.540 ms`, versus `50.826/51.845 ms`, because it is already `7.7-8.7 ms` behind after the EP4 forward. Before loss, rank 8 emits `1,075` GPU kernels versus `893` on either sampled full-replica rank and has `38.766 ms` of all-stream idle/dependency gaps versus `24.158/28.589 ms`; this is consistent with 32 experts/GPU fragmenting the same nominal token load across more small expert operations. Reducing the reduced-replica batch is therefore not expected to remove this bottleneck; MBS is already 1 and GBS 6 gives exactly one microbatch per each of the six data-parallel lanes, so reducing it further would require idle/uneven lanes and would make expert GEMMs smaller.
- EP8/EP6 is a valid larger-reduced-replica experiment with `TP=2`: use nonuniform topology `4 3`, 14 GPUs, MBS1/GBS7, and compare against healthy topology `4 4`, 16 GPUs, MBS1/GBS8. NEP placement requires the expert count to divide both 8 and 6, hence a multiple of `lcm(8, 6) = 24`; `120` is the closest valid count to the current 128. This gives 15 experts/GPU on EP8 and 20 on EP6, versus 16/32 in the current 128-expert EP8/EP4 case, and should substantially reduce reduced-replica expert fragmentation. Both healthy and NEP cases must use 120 experts for a valid performance comparison.
- Kernel-type attribution strengthens, but does not fully prove, the fragmentation diagnosis. Before loss, ranks 0/4 each execute 227 NVJet GEMMs while reduced EP4 rank 8 executes 419: exactly 192 additional GEMMs, matching `16` additional local experts times six MoE slots times two expert linears. Every other major category has the same count except two additional fills and 12 fewer miscellaneous kernels. Rank-8 GEMMs average only `18.308 us` versus `29.069/29.700 us` on ranks 0/4, and their aggregate residency rises by only about `1.0 ms` (`7.671` versus `6.599/6.742 ms`), so the remaining pre-loss delay is chiefly launch/dependency spacing around those extra small GEMMs. This makes expert fragmentation a high-confidence cause of rank 8 sampled `7.7-8.7 ms` lag, but not yet a proven explanation for the entire `35.55 ms` job-level regression; owner Gather/EDP work and unprofiled-rank synchronization remain contributors. The controlled EP8/EP6 A/B is needed to measure how much job-level parity this removes.
- The workload already uses `--moe-router-force-load-balancing`, but this is statistical rather than exact balancing: `RandomSTE` replaces logits with rank-specific normal random values before top-k routing. Perfect deterministic balance could reduce residual token-count and EP-rank straggler variance, but it would not remove the structural fragmentation observed here. EP4 would still launch 32 local experts versus 16 on EP8, including the measured 192 additional expert GEMMs across six MoE slots. Exact balance is therefore expected to provide a secondary improvement at most; the larger reduced EP directly reduces the launch count. All future profiler experiments will capture every participating rank.
- Work assignment should follow measured replica throughput rather than GPU count alone. The current EP8/EP4 assignment is four versus two samples (`2:1`), which gives equal nominal samples and routed tokens per GPU. Using the sampled pre-loss spans (`50.6-51.6 ms` full for four samples versus `59.1 ms` reduced for two) gives a rough throughput-weighted target of about `2.3:1` full-to-reduced work. Prefer adding full-replica samples to consume otherwise idle capacity rather than reducing the already MBS1 reduced work, which makes expert GEMMs still smaller and discards global throughput. Either direction requires heterogeneous per-replica microbatch scheduling plus sample-count-aware gradient normalization; the current static Megatron schedule cannot directly express the fractional target. EP8/EP6 remains the simpler structural experiment before adding that scheduler.
- Only ranks 0/4/8 were profiled. They prove rank 4 and rank 8 are specific late participants in the sampled owner-critical waits, but cannot identify whether unprofiled owners 1-3 or followers 5-7 are later on other collectives. A complete peer attribution requires traces from ranks 0-10 in the relevant TP lane.

Several source buckets already cross adjacent MoE-layer boundaries.
- Approach A currently discards those source bucket boundaries when it rebuilds expert groups by logical parameter slot. The native owner path therefore reduced 12 separate `159,645,696`-element FP32 tensors (`609 MiB` each) per step, exactly `fc1` and `fc2` for each of six MoE layers. Changing `--ddp-num-buckets` alone cannot coalesce these NEP reductions.
- To test multi-layer bucketing, NEP must aggregate consecutive logical slots into owner-layout native DDP buckets, retain per-slot Gather readiness, launch one EDP reduction when the aggregate bucket becomes ready, and Scatter its slots afterward. Earlier aggregate buckets can overlap with remaining backward compute; an all-model bucket would instead become ready only at the backward tail and expose all of its communication, so the useful experiment is a small number of multi-layer buckets rather than one unlimited bucket.
- Clarified that the per-slot regrouping is an implementation mistake relative to the requirement to use Megatron native DDP, not an intended NEP property. The refactor reused Approach A's old slot builder and called native `_ParamAndGradBucketGroup.start_grad_sync()` on a new synthetic tensor, but it did not preserve Megatron's source bucket objects, bucket boundaries, parameter readiness, or `param_to_bucket_group` mapping. The correction must follow NTP more literally: wrap the existing expert bucket groups, create a participant-consistent owner-layout view for each native bucket, let native bucket readiness trigger EDP sync, and launch post-sync Scatter from that same bucket lifecycle.
- Megatron DDP already keeps expert and non-expert parameters separate. Parameters with `param.allreduce == False` are placed in `expert_parallel_buffers`, partitioned into `expert_parallel_bucket_groups`, and reduced on the expert-DP group; all other parameters use `buffers`/`bucket_groups` and the DP-CP group. In job `2406146`, NEP had three non-expert bucket groups and seven expert bucket groups. The native-bucket NEP correction should wrap only the seven expert groups and leave dense/shared/router synchronization unchanged.
- Current Approach A does not in fact leave non-expert DDP behavior fully unchanged. Before parent DDP construction it MAX-synchronizes the locally derived bucket threshold across the NEP DP topology, which changed job `2406146` from the healthy `94,486,908`-element threshold/four non-expert groups to `154,354,044` elements/three non-expert groups. It also overrides the backward post-hook so native non-expert buckets only record readiness; their `start_grad_sync()` calls are deferred until `finish_grad_sync()` after NEP expert work drains. Their bucket objects and DP-CP communicator remain native, but their partitioning and overlap schedule are changed. ## 2026-07-15 - Post-graph device-aligned phase scheduler

- The 14-stage `MEMEM*EMEMEM*E` result establishes the new optimization target: ordered-split EP8/EP4 reaches `88.90%` clean per-GPU throughput parity, with a `17.54 ms` healthy-to-NEP gap. Native model-EP and dense-DP collectives are not systematically inflated; trace-matched early participant residency instead adds `16.0-17.4 ms/step` on follower Scatter and `7.0-12.4 ms/step` on selected reduced-owner EDP calls.
- Implemented an opt-in `MEGATRON_NONUNIFORM_EP_POST_GRAPH_PHASES=1` scheduler on top of split host phases. A non-MoE local CUDA graph post-replay hook runs only after useful backward compute has been queued, waits local Gather device completion before the EDP-owner Gloo rendezvous, records and waits EDP device completion before the owner/follower Scatter rendezvous, then launches Scatter. All ProcessGroup calls remain on the autograd thread and the existing completion event is still consumed before the next model-EP collective.
- Added unique non-MoE graph-manager selection so MoE-containing graph replays cannot advance the prior layer pipeline. Added focused tests for graph-manager filtering, Gather/EDP device-aligned call order, and preservation of the model-EP completion fence. Local Python compilation and `git diff --check` pass; the login node has no `uv`.

## 2026-07-15 - Split host-phase scheduler implementation

- Started the requested EP8/EP4, 2-4 layer debugging cycle. The stable pair-host path remains the default; the experiment is opt-in through `MEGATRON_NONUNIFORM_EP_SPLIT_HOST_PHASES=1` with device and same-communicator readiness gates disabled.
- Split the ProcessGroup dispatch boundary into two ordered host phases. The MoE gradient-ready callback enqueues Gather and asynchronously submits the owner-transfer and EDP-owner Gloo rendezvous, then returns to autograd. The next model-EP boundary waits those already-submitted rendezvous, enqueues EDP and the pre-Scatter pair rendezvous, enqueues Scatter, records completion, and inserts the existing CUDA event dependency before model-EP work.
- Added explicit DDP state for a Gather-launched-but-not-yet-scattered boundary. Expert buckets are no longer required to report ready until the deferred EDP/Scatter phase completes; completion is then checked before the event is recorded. The split path falls back to the stable inline path when task batching would reuse a communication-buffer slot.

## 2026-07-15 - Representative layer-level slowdown attribution

- Compared healthy job `2322588` rank-0 trace with pair-host NEP job `2333379` ranks 0/4/8. The profiled steps averaged `426.48 ms` healthy and `658.67 ms` NEP (`1.54x`); this is larger than the clean iteration ratio (`463.85 / 322.75 = 1.44x`), so the trace is used for attribution rather than the final throughput ratio.
- Reconstructed the 23 MoE layers from the 46 grouped-linear backward events per step. All 22 complete MoE-to-MoE backward windows were slower under NEP: median ratio `2.07x`, range `1.72-2.51x`, and median additive cost `8.50 ms`. The four depth quartiles were `2.03x`, `2.09x`, `2.01x`, and `2.08x`, showing that the slowdown is distributed uniformly through model depth rather than concentrated in a few layers. These windows account for `185.18 ms` of the `232.19 ms` profiled-step delta (about `80%`).
- CUDA graph execution itself was effectively unchanged: aligned median NEP/healthy execution-span ratios were `1.005x` for Mamba and `1.001x` for attention; router graph kernel time was also `1.005x` at the median. The delay is inserted around/between graph execution: median launch-to-first-kernel delay grew `1.81x` for Mamba and `4.40x` for attention. Owner rank 0, follower rank 4, and reduced-owner rank 8 had nearly identical total step spans and MoE-window medians, so the regression is a synchronized per-MoE-boundary communication/scheduling cost, not slower layer math or one localized straggler layer.
- Code/trace correlation clarifies that the extra existing-Megatron NCCL time is primarily scheduler serialization and participant-arrival skew, not demonstrated raw bandwidth interference. Each layer Gather, EDP reduction, and Scatter are enqueued serially on one shared NEP dispatch stream; `_wait_for_nep_dispatch_launch()` then makes the compute/current stream wait on the layer completion event before the next model-EP boundary. The overlapping participant sets differ (`nep_owner_transfer` pair `[0,4]`, `ep_dp` pair `[0,8]`, regular EP group `[0-7]`), so pair/owner barriers align local phases but can deliver the four pairs to the next full EP collective at different times. An early EP NCCL kernel then records long residency while waiting for the other EP ranks.
- Dense-DP overlap is explicitly disabled for the NCCL NEP path: parameter hooks record dense readiness without calling the normal Megatron `start_grad_sync`, and `_start_delayed_dense_grad_syncs()` launches all dense buckets only from `finish_grad_sync()` after the NEP drain. Its extra tail is therefore an implementation constraint, not evidence that reshard traffic made the same dense all-reduce intrinsically slower. `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` may add cross-communicator ordering pressure, but the current evidence does not isolate it as the dominant performance cause; CUDA connection count is not causal on Blackwell.

## 2026-07-08 - EP4/3 helper-launch ordering diagnosis

- Job `2319798` retried the three-rank owner-transfer groups with first-batch transfer-member phase synchronization. It still stalled because a helper's variable-split ProcessGroup Gather had zero input and output, so synchronizing its CUDA stream did not fence collective completion. The follower advanced to Scatter while the owner remained in Gather.
- Switched the first batch to the same fixed-count native CE Gather/Scatter used by steady state. Job `2319821` completed a finite first iteration in `5647.3 ms`, proving that first-batch helper phases were now ordered, but iteration 2 timed out in model EP `ALLTOALL_BASE` sequence 40 on full-replica ranks 0, 1, and 3.
- Added rank/role and host-call timing around native Gather/Scatter, then ran all-rank diagnostic job `2319878` on the same seven-GPU EP4/3 topology. It reproduced the iteration-2 timeout and identified the cycle:
  - rank 2, a zero-payload helper for owner 1, entered owner-1 Gather before owner/source rank 1 was gradient-ready;
  - the direct native call returned in `0.228 ms`, so the Python host thread was not blocked;
  - owner/source rank 1 entered model EP all-to-all sequence 40 before its owner-1 Gather, while rank 2's earlier CE Gather prevented rank 2 from joining that all-to-all;
  - the failure is therefore a cross-communicator GPU launch-order cycle caused by empty-entry helper readiness, not replica skew or a five-minute native-call delay.
- Added a per-owner/chunk pre-Gather Gloo readiness gate and validated it with job `2319924`; import formatting, Black, and all 15 focused tests passed. Runtime job `2319956` showed that this was still unsafe: all owner-0 ranks passed the host gate, but the background Gather launch raced the next model collective in different rank orders and its CUDA event never completed.
- Moved readiness to a whole-bucket inline barrier and validated the revised state machine with job `2319995`; all 16 focused tests passed. Runtime job `2320022` then showed why any blocking parameter/bucket hook is unsafe: helper rank 2 waited in owner-1 pre-Gather barrier while ranks 1 and 3 still needed rank 2 in a later model EP all-to-all.
- Compared the NEP launch path with NTP. NTP can launch directly from parameter post-hooks because reshard and model tensor-parallel work share one communicator and therefore one collective order. NEP owner-transfer groups are distinct from the model EP communicator, so its safe launch point is after an MoE layer dispatch all-to-all backward has completed.
- Replaced the parameter-hook launch with a `BaseMoELayer` full-backward boundary hook. Each layer now launches its ready zero-SM pipelines in global task order as source-host barrier, native Gather, launch barrier, EDP-host barrier and all-reduce, source-host barrier, then native Scatter. Gather, EDP reduction, and Scatter remain enqueued on the same NEP CUDA stream so they can overlap the next layer backward compute without overtaking the current layer final EP collective.
- Validation job `2320112` spent about `2m47s` importing the NeMo 26.06 image and timed out before producing a test result. This setup duration, like the earlier five-minute watchdog interval, is not rank-arrival skew. The identical rerun `2320194` on the warmed node completed in `1m20s`; all 16 focused tests passed in `0.97s`.
- Runtime job `2320213` completed the seven-GPU EP4/3 smoke in `3m17s` including cold-node startup. All three iterations were finite with zero skips and NaNs; steady-state iteration 3 was `93.3 ms`. Iterations 2-3 traversed 144 matched before/after source Gather and Scatter stages and 96 matched before/after EDP stages, with no stranded task or finish-time communication tail.

Rank 0 spent `203.8 ms` in 448 blocking Gloo barriers across the two profiled iterations; rank 3 spent `137.1 ms` in 576. The barriers ran inside the autograd hook, so next-layer kernels could not be enqueued while reshard ran.

Every rank still walks the same global owner/chunk sequence on the single NEP stream. Healthy ranks had four dense groups with `299,945,984`, `302,388,192`, `302,388,192`, and `200,870,240` elements; reduced ranks had two with `531,236,512` and `574,356,096` elements. Both layouts total exactly `1,105,592,608` elements, but collective counts and boundaries differ. The job was canceled after this proof.
- Root cause is `--ddp-num-buckets 16`: training derives `bucket_size` from each rank's total local parameter count. Reduced-EP ranks hold more local expert parameters, so they derive a larger bucket size even though the dense parameter sequence is identical across replicas.
- Added a pre-DDP synchronization for NEP runs when `num_buckets` is configured. Each dense DP group takes the maximum locally derived bucket size before constructing buffers, producing identical dense bucket boundaries while retaining bucketing. Corrected first-batch readiness validation to use complete local parameter coverage because golden ready-count maps are populated only after the first reset.

- Job `2291821` completed both iterations with finite loss and zero skipped/nan iterations. The local bucket-size derivations were `298,590,226` elements on healthy ranks and `528,080,914` on reduced ranks; synchronization selected `528,080,914` everywhere, and all sampled ranks built the identical two dense buckets of `531,236,512` and `574,356,096` elements. This removed the NCCL operation-count mismatch.

Each such hook contained roughly 2,700 tensor-slice dispatches, 900 copies, 300 adds, and 300 scales, so copy-engine operations usually finished before autograd could submit the next compute kernel.

## 2026-07-02 - Lyris NEP overlap investigation

- Completed corrected eight-bucket Lyris comparisons using nvcr.io/nvidia/nemo:25.09: healthy MBS2 job 2261389, NEP MBS2 job 2261369, healthy MBS4 job 2261390, and NEP MBS4 job 2261391.
